html:
Appearance

Polly Janet Harvey was a pretty philistine: blond hair below the shoulders, cornflower eyes, thin light eyebrows. When Joaquin first saw her in Izluchina, she wore a brown woolen dress with lace on her chest and a white blouse with rolled sleeves that opened fragile wrists. Later, Harmon admired the way the sun's rays sparkled in her blond strands.

Origins

Polly was from Niar. According to her, she grew up in a city that can be bypassed on foot in an hour, and only the nobles kept the horses there. Her brothers held a tavern where she sang. There she heard John, a woodcarver, "the best in Niar", and chose the bride from the first meeting. He almost did not remember Polly himself: before the wedding, they met only once, when he came to her city for the fair, and after the wedding he left for the workshop from dawn. They lived together for a year and “never seemed to speak for themselves.” The couple lived on the second floor of the house, and on the first held a workshop. Polly helped her husband: she drew sketches with a pencil, and John repeated them with a cutter. In the spring of 1774, she was a widow for only two weeks. What John died of, she didn't say. Fleeing from the blue sea, she was going to her cousins in Elfort on the Wise River, in the north of the Southern Way. (Blue-Grey Plague)

Meeting with the train

On the evening of April 12, 1774, in the hotel tavern of Izluchina, drunken craftsmen pestered a lonely girl. (Riverbend) Joaquin Eve Hannah stood up for her ("If you want to say something to my lady, first tell me") and gave her dinner. Polly asked to train, saying that she knows how to sew, cook and knows “dozens and three” songs. Then Joaquin frowned, let go of his hands and got a ringing slap. In the morning Polly and the other refugees got into the van. Harmon found out that she was a widow, and only she one of the refugees caused him sympathy. Polly was not interested in talking about the gray sea: she embroidered flowers on the hem of a Sarafan and repeated the covenant of St. Yangmei: “Burn quietly, and rejoice loudly.”

On the second night, Polly sang, and she sang in her own way. She did not lead the song like other singers, but "followed her", changing her voice after saying, "Polly lived someone else's life while she sang." She was forced to remember two dozen songs. Even the sullen Snape gave something flattering, and Doxet gave a meditative speech. Soon, the young grandson of the old Painter had blue lips, and the companions demanded to expel his grandfather and boy in the rain. Polly firmly said that it was a cold: “I saw how they die from the blue sea.” She slept with the boy in the van, gave him hot wine, and she was right. After that, Harmon offered her to ride with the train for a couple of months with a cook, a seamstress and a singer. Polly didn't even ask about the fee, only what places they would see.

With Joaquin

The first days Joaquin deliberately did not notice Polly, and she answered him with “reciprocity”. Then he apologized for the Izlyuchin, and they switched to "you".

At the end of April 1774, the train entered the Southern Way. Going to sell the Light Sphere to Count Vittor Shayland, Harmon left carts and horses under the care of Snip and Louise, and himself sailed on a schooner across Smoky Dahl Lake to Waymar on 8 May, taking only Joaquin and Polly with him. (Smoky Distance) On the deck Polly admired jugs, asked about the recent wedding of the count with Iona Origin, dreamed of seeing the bride and was interested in gifts for the owner of the castle, and in the evening at the request of sailors sang songs about ships and the sea. Harmon noticed that he and Joaquin were watching, and for the first time regretted taking her with him. At the count's castle Polly as a servant dined in the kitchen with a man, and Joaquin sat at the table and after a bad fight in the castle remained bruised. When asked by Polly how he liked the Northern Princess, he replied, "Her background does not allow me to say bad things about her," and she decided that Lady Iona was a bad person. For two days, Polly was making him a parka, and on the way back, she rubbed ointment into his battered ribs. It was then that Harmon realized that Polly was not like the calculating mature women he was used to, and that he cared about her. After returning to the train, in May, Polly admitted that she had never sat in the saddle, and Joaquin began to teach her horseback riding, sitting in front of him on the mare. After straying off the road to Soltown, the train lost two days and came across the hunters of the local lord, Sir Ben Womack. (Benjamin Womack) Under the pretext of checking for the gray sea, the squires told the travelers to undress, and the lord's squire had already pulled tights on Polly's corsage when Joaquin rushed at Ser Womack, wounded him, and forced the hunters to let the girl go and lay down their weapons. The train ran in the spring rain, and the morning after the fight, Polly and Joaquin became lovers. Harmon, who also fell in love with Polly, was jealous. In Soltown, he gave her vanilla perfume from the south, and out of inexperience, she suffocated so that at dinner they all noticed: “Now I will smell like a lady.” Joaquin was offended, and reconciled their scallop, which Harmon advised him to buy.

The break came under the Labelin. Over dinner, everyone talked about their dreams. Polly said that after the sea will return to Niar, where her husband left her a house and a workshop, find apprentices and, "give the gods", will meet a good man. She hoped for two sons and two daughters, and at these words she patted herself on the stomach significantly. Joaquin slept off his face and left to "clean the mail." Polly realized that he despises the life she dreams of, and that he loves "the lady from the page", a newspaper portrait of Lady Alanis. The first time she saw the train, she clapped her hands and begged to wait for another train. Harmon has already decided that he will marry her, “if he did not suffer from a good boy.” In mid-June, while waiting for a response from the Sphere's buyer, Baron Darryl, Harmon would ride Polly in a breech around town (Joaquin got a place on the goats), show her a two-story white limestone mansion selling from the windows of which trains were visible, and hinted that he would buy it and would like her to stay in his service. (Hugo Derrill) Polly was amazed and genuinely pleased for him. On the way, Joaquin quarreled with Harmon and left the service; Polly followed him, but stayed.

Salvation of Harmon

In mid-June 1774, armed men stole Harmon from the hotel at night. Polly woke up from the noise, jumped on a horse and followed. Harmon himself in captivity, remembering his men, asked the kidnappers whether they and the girl Polly were alive. In the city it was guided by sound, and outside the city on the wavy trail of a wheel rolling. So she found the ruins of a fortress ten miles north of Labelin and saw six guards there. She guessed that the door at the base of the tower descent into the dungeon: there entered with torches even during the day. Then she found Joaquin at the railway station, judging that he, although he says that he does not like trains, says this "with a very dreamy look." There she broke up with him: “I’m not a couple, and you’re me. We will not be happy together.” And ashamed of his pride, recalling that a real knight would save the suzerain “even from the mouth of the Dark Ido.” Joaquin agreed, and with Doxet and Snipe released the host. When the exhausted Harmon was brought to the wagon, Polly and Louise hugged him, lamented over him and persuaded to wash and change into clean clothes.

When Harmon's men were preparing a raid on the Maximian monastery, Polly herself asked for intelligence: she had seen only one Sacred Object in her life and wanted to look at another. In order not to stand out among the pilgrims, she came up with the idea of playing blessed. Her smile became scattered, the look passed through the interlocutor, and the look, despite the cuteness, came out “creepy”. When Polly came back, she was the first to say that monks are villains. Monks are always serene, and the faces here are “stress and hidden anxiety”. Then, remembering her husband's craft, she cut out a copy of the Duke of Labelin's seal with dolphins on the bank bill, which was sealed with a fake letter. Before the last trip for the Sphere, Harmon tried to explain himself to her in love and called her to take a train to Faunterra. Polly was delighted, but decided that it was a trade trip, and asked how to load the wagons. Harmon never said anything. She wished him good luck and promised to pray for him.

Death

On July 4, 1774, the train returned with a wounded Joaquin and Whirlwind, followed by the monks. Polly warmed the wine and helped wash the wounds. Snape took the sum with the Light Sphere and went to the horse. (Radiant Sphere) At this moment Polly came out of the van with a pitcher: “Master, why do you need a weapon?” Snape grabbed her, put a knife to her throat, and took her away as a hostage, promising to let her go a mile away from the camp. Harmon fired a crossbow, though Joaquin shouted, "Don't shoot! You're going to hurt Polly!" A heavy bolt sewn through Snape and exited Polly between his ribs, above his left chest. Harmon took the Sphere and left, and the wounded Joaquin shouted to him after him: "Wife-killer!" The remaining men of the wagons buried Polly and prayed for everyone except for the escaped Harmon. Later, when Joaquin recovered from his wounds and again rushed to the war, Louise reproached him: “Three good men died, and with them your favorite!”

Legacy

Harmon confessed to Father David that he knew he could kill her by shooting her: the master who sold him a crossbow showed him how he punched through the lats. He stopped getting on trains because they were "too close to Polly's image." Later, he muffled thoughts about her, thinking about Niza, and in a dream he was pursued by a bolt in the girl's chest. He recalled walking with Polly on the Labelin and how she sang "Ballad of Teresa." In May 1775, at the bottomless failure, telling without concealing the story of the Light Sphere, Harmon named Polly among the dead and spoke of her most, "for it was demanded by conscience": how she sang, how she helped him, how fearlessly she went to scout and how she died with a bolt in her chest. The only hilt once spent on perfume for her seemed to him more valuable than all the later riches. Once, having drunk with Salem, Harmon even scolded her “smoky blind” for choosing Joaquin, not him. It was in that depth of intoxication, "where it is already slightly pulling to spit on dead bones."

Joaquin blamed himself for getting cold with Polly and abandoning her. In the autumn of 1774, while driving around Smallden, he cried, remembering her; to tell new acquaintances how Polly died before his eyes, he never decided. In March 1775, looking at the peasant market in the Lands of the Crown, he recalled Polly and Alanis together, and later persuaded himself that "not one in the world Polly." He long dreamed of a simple decent girl, and Harmon called the one who “shot Polly”. In 1775, while mourning the dead girls, Joaquin placed her name on a par with Laura and Gwenda.

Personality

Kind, reasonable and proud, Polly did not tolerate self-pity and did not want to be a burden: “Yes, I am a petty bourgeois, but pride is not alien to me, do you believe?” She was observant and decisive, well versed in people and was not afraid to go against the crowd. She loved trains, dreamed of her husband, children and a workshop and did not allow grief to take over.

Trivia

  • Lady Karen in the collector’s edition of “Arrow, Coin, Spark” calls Polly the most sympathetic heroine of the line of Coins. (Arrow, Coin, Spark (Collector's Edition)) She searched for information about her in Labelin, Niara and Izluchina, but did not find anyone who knew the girl, and admits that the author made her up.
  • Polly spoke about her hometown in different ways: she called Niar her native, but recalled that John came to my city to the fair before the wedding.

Appearances

  • "Arrow, Coin, Spark" - the heads of Harmon ("Coin") from the 7th to the 45th: The bend, a trip to Waymar, the way to Soltown and Labelin, the salvation of Harmon, death.
  • He is mentioned in Joaquin and Harmon's memoirs in Only One Star, A Doll on the Throne, The Yanmei Hunt, and The Shadow of the Great Tree.
